speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: With Monday's deadline looming for Iraqis to come up with a draft      constitution, several major issues remain unresolved.  One of the most      contentious is this:  Should Iraq be a unified country with a strong      central government, or a confederation of three largely autonomous      regions, one for Kurds in the north, another for Sunni Arabs in the      center of the country and a third for Shiites in the south?  This is the      federalist approach.  Fueling the debate, the head of a powerful Iraqi      Shiite group today demanded a large, autonomous Shiite zone that would      encompass half the country's population.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: We're going to hear two views now on the future shape of the Iraqi state.      Leslie Gelb joins us.  He's president emeritus of the Council on Foreign      Relations, and he favors a decentralized federalist approach.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: Welcome, Mr. Gelb.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Hi.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: And also, Judith Yaphe, senior research fellow at National      Defense University, an advocate for a strong central Iraqi government.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: Thanks for being with us.

speaker_label: Ms. JUDITH YAPHE (Senior Research Fellow, National Defense University)
text: You're welcome.  Thank you for inviting me.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: Les Gelb, I want to start with you.  You think that what would      amount essentially to some kind of partition of Iraq into three      autonomous is a good idea.  Why so?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Well, there are two points that I would make.  One, I think,      the paradox is that the only way I can think of to keep the country      together, keep it one country, is to make it as decentralized as      possible.  That's the only thing the three major groups, I believe, in      the end, will tolerate.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: The second reason is a federal plan with decentralized power is the only      way I can think of now to work out a peace deal among the three major      parties, because in the end, no one of them is going to let the others      dominate it. But if you let each group legislate essentially for itself,      I think they'd buy into a united Iraq and to that constitution.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: Judith Yaphe, with all of these competing interests in Iraq, why      do you think a strong centralized government can bring them together?

speaker_label: Ms. JUDITH YAPHE (Senior Research Fellow, National Defense University)
text: There are some things that Les and I agree on and I think      that's the end point, which is not a partitioned Iraq.  But I disagree      with what comes before that, because I don't think this will make Iraq      more secure nor will Iraqis feel more secure and happy.

speaker_label: Ms. JUDITH YAPHE (Senior Research Fellow, National Defense University)
text: Now I will argue on two points that Les made.  First of all, do the--the      Sunnis don't want partition.  I'm not sure that the majority of Shia do,      either.  They identify federalism and this kind of decentralization with      virtual partition and that's not something that I've heard Iraqis want.      Arab Sunni, Arab Shia--they don't identify themselves in those strong      sectarian terms except for the extremists in the south around Basra,      who--the one cleric who did is head of the Supreme Council for the      Islamic Revolution in Iraq, which leads me to my second point.  Would      this make Iraq safer?  No.  If you have decentralized government in these      provinces, it's going to make them more open to foreign manipulation.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: Les Gelb, Judith Yaphe there mentioned foreign manipulation.      Isn't there an argument there, that if the state is divided into three      zones, strength in unity is gone and the neighbors--Turkey, Syria,      Iran--could all be nibbling at an Iraq that's divided into parts?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Sure.  Judith made all good points, and I start from the point      that the situation in Iraq is very dire and it's getting worse and we      have to do the best we can, which isn't going to be very good.  I think      if we tried to stuff all these three groups into an Iraq with a strong      central government, they wouldn't buy it and Iraq would end up splitting      apart in a civil war.  I don't want that.  That's why I say I think the      paradox is the only way to keep them together is to decentralize as much      as possible.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: Judith Yaphe, isn't the idea of a unified Iraq really something      of a historical artifact?  This country was cobbled together by the      British back in the 1920s.  Why should that be the model for what we      should do now?

speaker_label: Ms. JUDITH YAPHE (Senior Research Fellow, National Defense University)
text: Well, I've always been upset when I hear that term because I      think it ignores much of the history.  Many of these places were under      the Ottoman Empire.  At one time, France and Germany and Italy were      cobbled together, weren't they?  So why do we make a major point of that      for Iraq when we haven't made it for anyplace else?  These were provinces      as part of the Ottoman system that lived together and worked together,      and many Iraqis had a very strong sense of nationalism going back to the      World War I period.  This is not something which was just created anew by      Saddam or invented by the Brits; it was there and it still is.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: Leslie Gelb.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yeah, I just didn't see much of Iraqi nationalism in my trip      there or in my conversations with Iraqis over the years.  Now when I ask      them what do they think themselves to be, most of them answer, you know,      Arab Sunni or Shia or Kurd, much more so than they say Iraqi.

speaker_label: Ms. JUDITH YAPHE (Senior Research Fellow, National Defense University)
text: That is interesting, Les.  I'm glad you said that.  You're      right. When one talks to Iraqi Kurds, they're Kurds first, Iraqi some      place second and...

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yes.

speaker_label: Ms. JUDITH YAPHE (Senior Research Fellow, National Defense University)
text: ...religion the last identifier they would think about.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yes.

speaker_label: Ms. JUDITH YAPHE (Senior Research Fellow, National Defense University)
text: But when I talk to the Arabs of Iraq, Sunni or Shia, and I      ask: `Who are you?'  Iraqis.  That's what I hear from the Iraqis I talk      to.  And when you find out--`Are you Sunni or Shia?'--that comes a little      bit later down the road.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: Just one last question for you both.  If this issue of how to      formulate the new Iraqi state is left vague in the Iraqi Constitution      because they can't figure out how to resolve it, what then?  How do you      come to terms with this?  Judith Yaphe.

speaker_label: Ms. JUDITH YAPHE (Senior Research Fellow, National Defense University)
text: The issue is that the Iraqis have a document that they can      agree on at that point, which gives them a baseline start and they move      from there. You're not going to have all of these things--right now they      know what the state looks like; they know their external borders.      Internally, they have to decide do they want 18 provinces, five, three,      whatever?  Do they want some form of federalism or not?  How do you      divide up the powers or not, the resources or not?  All of those issues.      They're going to have to do some hard trading if they want to avoid civil      war.

speaker_label: Ms. JUDITH YAPHE (Senior Research Fellow, National Defense University)
text: Les is right.  The situation is terrible.  It is dire.  But I do have a      little bit of hope against my Iraqis and your Iraqis.  But the point is      that they're talking and trying to find some resolution.  And they've      suffered so much that I think they want to move ahead, so I have to be a      little bit optimistic.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yeah, I agree with Judith.  I think we have to give them a      little more running room, but I think they are going to have to resolve      most of these issues within some weeks or some months.  Otherwise, this      is going to break out into civil war.

speaker_label: Ms. JUDITH YAPHE (Senior Research Fellow, National Defense University)
text: Yeah.

speaker_label: MELISSA BLOCK, host
text: Two views of the future of the Iraqi state from Leslie Gelb,      president emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations, and Judith Yaphe,      senior research fellow at National Defense University.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: And more now on the president's speech.  We're joined by longtime foreign      policy expert Leslie Gelb.  He's a former high official at the      departments of State and Defense.  He's now president emeritus at the      Council on Foreign Relations.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: Mr. Gelb, welcome to the program.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Good      afternoon.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: Your overall reaction to the speech, sir?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Good step forward in explaining his strategy, a good step      forward in increased honesty and in owning up to past mistakes.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: I was interested to hear Mr. Bush compare Iraq to Japan in the      Second World War and the resolve of President Truman.  Here's that      portion of the president's speech.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: President GEORGE W. BUSH:  Like today, there were many skeptics and      pessimists who said that the Japanese were not ready for democracy.      Fortunately, President Harry Truman stuck to his guns.  He believed, as I      do, in freedom's power to transform an adversary into an ally.  And      because he stayed true to his convictions, today, Japan is one of the      world's freest and most prosperous nations and one of America's closest      allies in keeping the peace.  The spread of freedom to Iraq and the      Middle East requires the same confidence and persistence, and it will      lead to the same results.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: Leslie Gelb, what do you think of that?  Is Japan a good      analogy for Iraq?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: I'm glad you picked that out because the president is fixated      on the Truman-Japan analogy, and I think it's entirely wrong.  We totally      conquered Japan like we conquered Iraq, but we threw Saddam out of power.      We kept Emperor Hirohito in power.  And Emperor Hirohito, in effect,      blessed the American occupation, which was a peaceful occupation.  He      blessed the transition to democracy, which was a consensus and peaceful      transition.  It was entirely different.  You know, what's more, under our      tutelage and under our protection, the Japanese did it.  And one of the      characteristics of Mr. Bush's speech today, and of the other speeches as      well, was that they were about we, the United States--we're going to win      the victory.  And I think that's one of the real flaws in the strategy      even as he presents it now.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: So you--do you not see any evolution in the president's      thinking in the war and in his message?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: No, I think there is an evolution.  In fact, I wish he had      given these speeches a year or so ago.  It would have put us in a better      position today.  But I think the speech still leaves us short on two of      the key elements of any successful strategy.  One is our troop      redeployments and withdrawals.  I'm not talking about any artificial      timetables here because I don't believe in that, but how do you use the      redeployments and withdrawals to convince the Iraqis that the war is      going to be their responsibility?  If you ask any of our military people,      they will tell you that's the key.  So we've got to use the withdrawals      in order really to impress on them that sooner rather than later they're      going to have to take on this responsibility.  And the president has got      to balance that pressure with the worry, legitimate worry, that if we      take the troops out too fast, it might lead to civil war. That's one      problem he didn't address in any serious way.  The other problem is that      he focuses on the elections.  And we like to focus on elections.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: He called this a watershed event tomorrow.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yeah, called it a watershed.  I, you know, wish it were.  I      wish he would be right.  But he called the January elections a watershed.      Purple power, everybody putting up purple fingers in the air.  And the      press and the administration saying this is a watershed, a turning point.      It wasn't.  And the elections aren't going to be that.  The elections      are a step.  Behind the elections is the constitution and the chance to      amend this constitution and bring about a power-sharing agreement among      the major religious and ethnic groups to settle this thing peacefully,      create some legitimacy, so that the soldiers have something to fight for.      And these issues--and these are the two gut issues, core issues--really      weren't addressed in the president's strategy.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: I said that you had served in the State Department...

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: I did.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: ...and that was during a Democratic administration.  Do you      hear Democrats putting forward a good alternative to what the president      is saying?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: I do not.  I think one of the real problems in this debate has      been that even though people are very skeptical about what the president      is saying, they haven't found the Democrats putting together any viable      or feasible alternative.  And as long as the Democrats don't, I think the      conclusion that most Americans reach is, well, as bad as Bush is doing,      it's not clear the Democrats would know what to do, either.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: Leslie Gelb, president emeritus at the Council on Foreign      Relations, joining us from New York City.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: Mr. Gelb, thank you for being with us on DAY TO DAY.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Always a pleasure.

speaker_label: ALEX CHADWICK, host
text: Stay with us on DAY TO DAY from NPR News.

speaker_label: STEVE INSKEEP, host
text: The latest fighting in the Middle East comes just a few weeks before a new American administration takes office. And to talk about what they might or might not be able to do, we're joined by Leslie Gelb. He's on the line from New York. He's a former U.S. diplomat, now with the Council on Foreign Relations. Welcome to the program.

speaker_label: Dr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Good to be here.

speaker_label: STEVE INSKEEP, host
text: Is it clear to you what the Obama administration's at least starting policy toward the Middle East is?

speaker_label: Dr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: I think it's a mystery to me and I suspect it's a mystery to them. I think we can bet that he's not going to be as pro-Israeli as the Bush administration has been. George Bush has been the most pro-Israeli president I think we've ever had. The Obama administration will be less so and try to steer more of a middle course between Israel and the Arab states. You know, we know a good deal about the Obama people going into this new administration, and they are more tilted toward Israel, but basically middle-of-the-roaders, with the exception of Hillary Clinton who is quite pro-Israel. And as for Obama himself, he's made the requisite pro-Israeli statements during the campaign, but we don't know what this guy's going to do. And I suspect he's going to surprise us in areas like Israeli-Palestinian negotiations.

speaker_label: STEVE INSKEEP, host
text: Does President-elect Obama have a reservoir of goodwill that he can draw on in the Arab world?

speaker_label: Dr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: I think that President Obama will start off his tenure with very positive feelings throughout the world. People want the United States to be the leader. They understand if we don't lead, nobody is going to be able to lead.

speaker_label: STEVE INSKEEP, host
text: Although I wonder is there a limited window for the president-elect? People are very hopeful on January 20th around the world, or in the Arab world, but if something that happens that they don't like on January 25th, it's all over.

speaker_label: Dr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: That's the way the press will put it. But it's up to President Obama to define his own priorities. And he is sitting on top of so many major problems, he cannot deal with them all simultaneously: Arab-Israeli, Syria, Iraq, Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Pakistan-India. You're going to have to do a kind of diplomatic triage and figure out the key one to start with and move from there.

speaker_label: STEVE INSKEEP, host
text: And persuade other people to be patient and wait?

speaker_label: Dr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: And persuade them to be patient and wait, even though they're going to start criticizing you the minute anything flares up in one of the areas that you're not treating as the topmost priority.

speaker_label: STEVE INSKEEP, host
text: Let me remember, because you're talking about interconnected problems. The Bush administration approached this thinking that if they solved one big problem, it might have an effect on others. And I may be oversimplifying here, but, for example, toppling Saddam Hussein, some people in the administration thought might make it easier to solve the Palestinian-Israeli conflict, might make it easier to deal with Iran, might make it easier to deal with Syria and get a lot of problems off the table over time. That's what they thought. Didn't precisely work out that way. But I wonder if you have any sense that people in the incoming administration think if we attacked this particular problem first, it's going to help us with the others?

speaker_label: Dr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yeah, I doubt that they'll choose Arab-Israeli to go first - that is the first place to really invest American power. They'll do something to start a diplomatic process because you can't let the Israelis and the Palestinians feel that we're neglecting them. So you've got to get a diplomatic and political process under way in that region. And in the case of the Palestinians and the Israelis, they've got to feel we have a way of changing the politics among the Palestinians and the Israelis so that there will be support for a deal.

speaker_label: STEVE INSKEEP, host
text: Although if you're saying as the Obama administration, you can't go first with the Arab-Israeli conflict, you have to solve these other problems first, isn't that conflict this constant irritant that makes it harder to deal with Pakistan, harder to deal with Muslims all over the world?

speaker_label: Dr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: There's no question that this infests everything else. And on the other hand, we're fighting two wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. And as I said, when you have so many first-order problems, you have to do a kind of national interest diplomatic triage. And in this case, it is not to ignore the Palestinian-Israeli situation, not in the least, but to set a process in motion that they will find a plausible way of solving it two, three, four years hence.

speaker_label: STEVE INSKEEP, host
text: Leslie Gelb of the Council on Foreign Relations, thanks for your insight.

speaker_label: Dr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: It's a pleasure.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: And now the Opinion Page, and the tangled motives of the various parties, following news last week of peace talks between the Afghan government of Hamid Karzai and elements of the Taliban. Some reports say Karzai is talking with Mullah Omar, the former leader of Afghanistan. Others suggest at least three different insurgent groups could be at the table. And, of course, both the United States and Pakistan have hands to play, as well.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: In a piece for The Daily Beast, Leslie Gelb concludes that the cynics may be right to conclude that little will come from these talks - at least this time around. Is it time to talk - as he writes - with the devil? Leslie Gelb is president emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations, and joins us by phone from New York. Nice to have you on the program.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Good afternoon.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: And it's important to remember these groups - you - we describe as the Afghan Taliban, are, as you describe, bad guys with a lot of American blood on their hands.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yes, they are. They really are bad guys. Just look at the way they ran Afghanistan when they were in charge. They could not have been more cruel. And you would think that that's reason enough for the Afghans themselves to fight like hell to defeat them. But, you know, the odd thing about this war is that we've become the main defenders of a free future for Afghans that they really ought to be defending for themselves.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: And the Obama administration - indeed, General Petraeus, who's now the military commander in Afghanistan - argue this is not the time to talk. We need to be in a stronger position, pummel the Taliban for a year or so, and then it might be time.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: That's basically the position of the administration, or at least - let me put it this way: Basically, the president - the position of president of the United States for Afghanistan, David Petraeus. The White House, I think, harbors - hopes that something could happen on this front. But basically, the White House goes along with the consensus that you don't start serious negotiations until you're in a stronger position.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: And so then what is our ally, Hamid Karzai, doing? Doing exactly that.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Well, he is playing games that suit his own purposes. His main purpose right now is to try to deflect American pressure on him to reform his government, and every once in a while, we decided to get tough with him. And one way he has of diffusing our pressure is to threaten to talk to the Taliban, because he knows we don't want him to do that now.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: And he knows we don't want him to do it now? So this is to get leverage with Washington.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: I think that's the main aim. Because, look, he understands full well that if he were to make any kind of deal with the Taliban on the issue that the Taliban demands most - namely withdrawal of all U.S. and NATO forces right away. If he were to make any kind of deal like that, he would be out of power the next day.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: Similarly, it seems unlikely the Taliban are likely to agree to the principal U.S. demand, which is that they renounce violence and renounce al-Qaida.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: You got it. So each side right now is making demands that the other side is entirely likely to reject.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: So why are the various Taliban elements - if all of them are there at the table - why are they talking? They can just play for time, they think.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yeah. I think they're talking - or at least some elements of the Taliban are talking. There's so many different Taliban groups. They're talking in order to create mischief, to create the notion in the minds of some Afghans that there might some deal reached to try to soften up the opposition. And they may be doing it, as well, to try to entice American opponents of the war.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: So to engender opposition to the war in the United States.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yeah. Or to make people feel that if we made a - the United States made a more generous offer to the Taliban, that some deal might be workable.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: Another player in the game, of course, Pakistan, which seems to be on both sides.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Well, at least on both sides. The Paks are the most difficult to understand and the easiest to understand in all of this. You would think, given all the public rhetorical explosions they make about the need for the United States to stay in Afghanistan to see that war through, that they would be strong backers of the United States. But, in fact, they tell us to stay in Afghanistan endlessly and they provide a safe haven for the Taliban and al-Qaida in Pakistan. They give them protection. They give them aid. And in these negotiations, on the one hand, they seem to be telling the Taliban go to it, do it, but we've got to be there to check on you.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: And their interest on that side of the table - well, really, their interest on both sides of the table is the longer term gain.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: I think so. But their interest is so conflicted because, you know, they do want us to stay there. And they do have their connection, a very deep one, to the Afghan Taliban. So, you know, they're on both sides of that issue.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: Another player in the game, not a direct one, but the party sponsoring the talks is the gulf state of Abu Dhabi, which you suggested...

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: (unintelligible)

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: ...might be the source of the story in the first place.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: That's right. They sponsored these talks, and they sponsored similar talks about a year ago. And mind you - and this is the measure of how serious these talks are - the press is allowed to sit in the room while the talks are going on. And some of the participants described the talks more as an academic seminar than as a negotiation. And I think that probably captures the spirit of the thing.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: So is there a time when it is going to be a - you suggest the cynics are right and given that context, it's likely that not much is going to emerge from these talks. But will there be a time when talks might be productive? And what would be the conditions then?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yeah. There almost always has to be - there's always has to be talks at some point, unless you're dealing with a real devil, somebody like a Hitler, and there's no making a deal with them. There's just looking after your own interests as best you can. But in this case, I think, there eventually will be talks.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: And look, every time we've been involved in some kind of clash, we end up talking to the other side. We talked to the North Koreans in order to have a ceasefire in the Korean War. And Vietnam, you know, we fought almost for a decade there. And Bob Gates is in Vietnam right now, and we're talking about joint military maneuvers - joint military maneuvers - with Vietnam against China. If we had understood anything about Vietnam years ago, we would have understood that they considered China their biggest adversary then, not just now.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: So, you know, there's a lot about these - in these countries, these cultures we don't begin to understand here. Americans aren't good in understanding what goes on in other countries. But at some point, if we are to extricate ourselves from Afghanistan while protecting our real interests there, it's going to involve talking to the Taliban devil.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: And you suggest General Petraeus - there's a telling quote about him sitting down to talk with people in Iraq who eventually helped the United States a great deal.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Exactly. I mean General Petraeus is one tough-minded guy. And even he said, when it came down to the wire in Iraq, you had to talk to the people who you were fighting if you wanted to get some deal that allowed us to extricate ourselves. And he said, you know, in the end, we're going to - we'll have to do that in Afghanistan as well. But I think it's got to be part of a strategy of protecting our interests there over the long run without fighting a major land war. That is what has to be in our head in order to be able to make a deal with the Taliban.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: You also point out domestic politics, of course, plays a role on all sides for Afghan President Karzai, for the Pakistanis, for the Taliban, certainly and...

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: That's what foreign policy is mainly about. Foreign policy is the extension of domestic politics by...

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: You're rewriting Clausewitz here.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yes.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: But there's also an element of American domestic politics as well. You write that the hawks in the United States are very worried by the prospect of these talks and the idea that important American national interests may be sold out.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Yeah. I mean, the problem with our debate on Afghanistan policy is that it hasn't been a serious debate at all. You know, in the first place, when we went in there 10 years ago - almost 10 years ago -there was good reason. Afghanistan was the home for the al-Qaida people who attacked us. So, sure, let's go in and get them.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: But all of the sudden, revenge, proper revenge turned into a major land war. And here we are, almost 10 years later, and what used to be the center of a threat to the United States, the terrorist threat to the United States in Afghanistan has now morphed so that that threat is even more serious from other parts of the world, from Pakistan, from Sudan, from Yemen, from Jersey City. So we have to really rethink the reasons for fighting in Afghanistan. It was once a very important interest. It's no longer anything resembling a vital interest in a war against terrorism.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: But there still will be a residual threat. And I think we have to figure out how to get our troops there down to a small and sustainable level to deal with that residual threat and begin to focus our energies on now the worldwide terrorist threat.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: Yet, some would argue that, indeed, we don't need necessarily to deal with the threat in Afghanistan so much as the threat that a defeat or a vacuum there would pose to Pakistan, a country which has nuclear weapons.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: I know. And I get that response every time I say what I just said to you, that, well, the war really isn't in Afghanistan. It's in Pakistan. And my answer to them is, sure, I think Pakistan is probably the country that represents the biggest threat to world peace and the safety of our friends and allies. It's a highly unstable country with a large extremist group and 100 nuclear weapons and building much more. So, you know, what do we do about that? I say to them, what are we going to do? They say, well, we'll work with them to create stability. We'll give them economic aid. It's a country of 180 million people that can't begin to govern itself and we're going to fix it up? That just won't happen.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: You know, and I think the best way to deal with the Pakistanis is to try to help the moderate group in that country by asking them what can we do to help strengthen your position. But if it involves any kind of open-ended stay in Afghanistan, I don't see how that begins to help the position of moderates in Pakistan. I don't get the connection.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: Leslie Gelb, thank you for your time today. Appreciate it.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council on Foreign Relations)
text: Sure.

speaker_label: NEAL CONAN, host
text: Leslie Gelb, president emeritus at the Council on Foreign Relations. He wrote an op-ed last week, "Dealing with the Devil" for The Daily Beast. You're listening to TALK OF THE NATION from NPR News.

speaker_label: ROBERT SIEGEL, host
text: Well, now to a critic of the Obama Afghan policy who says the White House should have revisited some basic questions. Leslie Gelb is president emeritus of the Council of Foreign Relations. Welcome to the program once again.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council of Foreign Relations)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: ROBERT SIEGEL, host
text: And what are some of the questions that you think a thorough review of Afghanistan policy should be addressing?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council of Foreign Relations)
text: There are two other broader sets of questions that have to precede any serious review of a foreign policy question. One is, sure, we face threats in Afghanistan and Pakistan, but are those threats as serious today as they were 10 years ago? Or have those threats morphed? Are they now all over the place and Afghanistan and Pakistan are no longer vital interests to the United States? That's the first question.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council of Foreign Relations)
text: And the second question is to look at ourselves. We have to ask, are these hundreds of billions of dollars we will spend on AfPak, as it's called, Afghanistan and Pakistan, over the next years worth it, given the terrible deteriorating economic situation in the United States? Can we afford to spend billions building roads and fixing schools in Afghanistan when the roads and schools are falling apart in America?

speaker_label: ROBERT SIEGEL, host
text: Let me ask you, though, an observation made in the assessment that was put out by the White House today. They say, al-Qaida's senior leadership in Pakistan is weaker - and I'm reading now - and under more sustained pressure than at any other point since it fled Afghanistan in 2001. You're saying yes, and that's one of the reasons why we should perhaps think differently about Afghanistan. But isn't that simply because there are more drone attacks, better intelligence and they're pursuing al-Qaida more effectively now than they were before?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council of Foreign Relations)
text: Yes. That's true. Whenever you put the U.S. military into a situation like that, they will punish the enemy. Our military is that good. But, you know, they can stay there forever. And as soon as they walk away, the situation can totally deteriorate.

speaker_label: ROBERT SIEGEL, host
text: What do you think of the feasibility of a U.S. handoff of combat responsibility to the Afghans sometime in 2014?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council of Foreign Relations)
text: Well, I think it depends on the thing we have least influence and control over, namely the effectiveness of the Afghan government. That will determine whether or not the Afghan army and Afghan police are really going to stand up and fight. They have to have something to fight for.

speaker_label: ROBERT SIEGEL, host
text: I remember once hearing many years ago, John Kenneth Galbraith, the one-time ambassador to India, economist, who said that in discussions in Washington about Vietnam policy, if you said, I think we should get out, if you said, I think we've had enough, we should leave Vietnam, you were no longer taken seriously in the discussion.

speaker_label: ROBERT SIEGEL, host
text: Do you think that the administration is at a point now when in order to be taken seriously in the discussion of what to do, you have to buy into the notion that we should be there big time with a big escalated force? Or is there still a voice within these discussions, as you know it, that might take a more dissenting view of the policy?

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council of Foreign Relations)
text: Well, that's an awfully good question and the answer is damning. I was a young man, director of policy planning in the Pentagon during the Vietnam War and I was a supporter of the war. And as I began to change and ask questions, I was very careful about how I put all this because right away you're ruled out of the discussion. And today, it's better than it was then, but it's still a problem.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council of Foreign Relations)
text: It's hard particularly inside the administration to ask the kind of fundamental questions that I'm suggesting must be asked in order to have a serious foreign policy.

speaker_label: ROBERT SIEGEL, host
text: A dissenting view from Leslie Gelb, president emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations. Les Gelb, thanks for talking with us once again.

speaker_label: Mr. LESLIE GELB (President Emeritus, Council of Foreign Relations)
text: Always a pleasure, Robert.
